readerTitle: Why Airbnb's founders knocked on doors in New York
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Airbnb, Stripe, Wufoo, Paul Graham 에세이) + 가상 적용 (동네 빵집)
insight: 초기에는 손으로 하는 일이 비효율이 아니라 첫 고객을 얻고 무엇을 자동화할지 배우는 가장 빠른 방법이다.
misconception: 처음부터 규모를 키울 수 있는 방식(광고, 자동화, 시스템)으로 시작해야 제대로 된 사업이다.

sources.text: Graham, P. (2013). Do Things that Don't Scale. paulgraham.com
Airbnb 공동창업자들의 초기 뉴욕 방문과 숙소 사진 촬영에 관한 인터뷰 및 강연 (Joe Gebbia 등)

factChecks.note: Airbnb 창업자들이 뉴욕에서 집집마다 방문해 새 호스트를 모집하고 기존 호스트의 숙소 소개를 개선했다는 내용은 Paul Graham(2013) 에세이에 나옵니다. 게시 전 원문을 다시 확인하세요.
창업자들이 직접 숙소 사진을 찍었고 이후 예약이 늘었다는 이야기는 창업자 인터뷰에 나오는 회고입니다. 매출이 '두 배'가 되었다는 등 구체적 수치는 출처마다 달라 카드에서 뺐습니다. 시기(2009년)도 확인하세요.
Stripe의 'Collison installation'(사용해 보겠다는 사람의 노트북을 받아 그 자리에서 설치)과 Wufoo의 손편지 감사 카드는 Paul Graham(2013) 에세이에 나옵니다. 인용 대신 풀어 썼습니다.
빵집 사례는 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why Airbnb's founders knocked on doors in New York
body: Around 2009, Airbnb was barely growing. Its founders had built a website anyone in the world could use.
So they did something that looked like a step backward. They flew to New York, visited hosts one at a time and took better photos of their apartments themselves.

image.label: Two founders with a camera at an apartment door
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 뉴욕 아파트 복도에서 카메라를 든 두 사람이 문 앞에 서 있고, 집주인이 문을 열며 반갑게 맞이함. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your marketplace has stalled.
body: You run a new website where people rent out spare rooms. You have a few hundred listings, and bookings are flat. Many listings have dark, blurry photos.
You have a little money and a lot of time. What do you do first?

options.text: Spend the money on online ads to bring in more guests
options.feedback: Ads bring visitors, but they land on the same weak listings. You pay for traffic without fixing why people don't book.

options.text: Build a tool that guides hosts to upload better photos
options.feedback: It could work later. But you'd be guessing what hosts struggle with, and building takes weeks you may not have.

options.text: Visit your best hosts in person and fix their listings yourself
options.feedback: It can't reach thousands of hosts, but it improves listings now and shows you exactly what a good listing needs.

cards.title: The slow way turned out to be fast.
body: The founders went door to door, signing up new hosts and helping existing ones improve their listings. They later said bookings rose after the new photos went up.
They also learned things no dashboard showed: what hosts worried about, what guests looked for, and why good homes didn't get booked.
Only later did Airbnb turn this into a program that sent photographers to hosts.

cards.title: Do things that don't scale
body: **Doing things that don't scale** means handling early customers by hand, in ways you could never repeat for a million of them.
Investor Paul Graham gave the idea its name in a 2013 essay. His point: new businesses rarely take off on their own. Founders have to recruit and delight the first customers one by one.

image.label: One customer at a time, then a system
image.brief: 왼쪽에는 창업자가 손님 한 명 한 명과 악수하는 작은 장면들, 오른쪽에는 같은 일을 하는 자동화된 컨베이어 장치. 가운데 화살표에 "Learn first, then automate" 라벨.

cards.title: Two things you get from the slow way.
body: Graham's essay gives more examples. Stripe's founders didn't just send a signup link. When someone agreed to try it, they asked for the person's laptop and set it up on the spot. Wufoo sent new users handwritten thank-you notes.
list: **Customers:** you win people who would never have found you or bothered to start
**Knowledge:** you see every problem up close, so you know what to fix and later automate
cards.callout: The manual work is a way to learn, not a way to run forever.

cards.title: Every corner shop already knows this.
body: A new café owner learns regulars' names and orders. A caterer drives the first trays over and stays to watch people eat. A repair business calls each customer the next day to ask if everything still works.
None of this scales to a hundred locations. But it turns strangers into regulars who bring friends, and it shows the owner what to put on the menu, the checklist or the training sheet.

image.label: Café owner greeting a regular by name
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 작은 카페. 주인이 카운터 너머로 단골 손님에게 이름이 적힌 컵을 건네며 웃는 장면. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: It's a phase, not a business model.
body: Manual work costs time, and time is your scarcest resource. If the business only works when you personally do everything, you haven't built a business yet.
Keep notes on what you do by hand and why. Each task should end in one of three ways: turn it into a system, hand it to someone else, or stop doing it.
And watch the costs. Spending heavily per customer is fine for learning, not as a permanent price of every sale.

cards.title: Now it's a neighborhood bakery.
body: Your bakery opened six weeks ago. People who try your bread come back, but too few people have tried it. Several office buildings are within a ten-minute walk.

options.text: Hire an agency to run social media ads across the whole city
options.feedback: You reach many people, but most live too far away to become regulars. It costs money before you know which customers stick.

options.text: Walk fresh samples into nearby offices each morning and ask what they'd order
options.feedback: It's slow and tiring, but it puts your bread in the right mouths and tells you what to bake. Later you can turn it into a standing office order.

options.text: Sign up with every delivery app right away
options.feedback: It makes ordering easier, but it doesn't make anyone try you first. Apps also take a cut of every early sale.

cards.title: Win the first customers by hand, then build the machine.
body: Early on, the work that can't scale is often the work that gets you customers and teaches you what to automate.
**Try it today:** pick one thing you could do personally for your next five customers that you could never do for five thousand. Do it, and write down what you learn.
